Mentor's note, second-year B.A., Thursday
Aditi came to see me after class. On Tuesday night the class meme page posted Manas's poem from the college magazine with mocking edits, and about sixty people piled in with comments. Aditi said she watched for an hour. 'I kept thinking someone else would say something. There were sixty of us.' Nobody did. At midnight she wrote one line: 'This is his real poem and he's in this group. Let's stop.' A few people agreed; the comments slowed and then stopped. Two people messaged her privately to say they had felt the same. Manas has not been to class since. I spoke with Manas today, told him none of this was his fault, and asked the page admins to remove the post. I've also informed the student welfare office. I told Aditi that one calm voice mattered.
Ishita

qa.q: How many people piled in with comments?
qa.a: About sixty people piled in with comments.

qa.q: Why did Aditi wait an hour before writing?
qa.a: With sixty people watching, Aditi assumed someone else would speak up, so the responsibility felt spread thin, even though she was uneasy.

qa.q: What made Aditi's one line effective?
qa.a: It was calm and specific, reminding everyone that Manas was real and in the group, which gave others permission to stop; the comments slowed and ended.

qa.q: What has the pile-on been like for Manas?
qa.a: Manas saw his own poem mocked by dozens of classmates and hasn't come to class since, which shows how humiliating it was.

grounding: Shows a mentor's note on a student who watched a class pile-on, waited for someone else to speak, and then broke the silence with one calm line.

passage:
Saturday
Tonight the hostel group turned on Reena. Someone posted a clip of her falling asleep in the lecture, and then it just grew: stickers, voice notes, a poll for 'most useless person in the batch'. I read everything. I didn't type anything. There were 140 people in that group. Someone would say something. Nobody did. I kept picturing Reena reading it in her room, alone.
At 11:40 I wrote: 'Reena is in this group and reading this. Can we delete it?' My thumb was shaking. For a minute, nothing. Then Farzana wrote 'agreed'. Then the admin deleted the poll.
I messaged Reena after. She said she'd been crying. I messaged the warden too, who called Reena straight away and said she would meet her at breakfast.
Joseph

qa.q: At what time did Joseph write in the group?
qa.a: Joseph wrote at 11:40.

qa.q: Why didn't Joseph type anything at first?
qa.a: With 140 people in the group, Joseph assumed someone else would speak up, so the responsibility felt spread out, even while picturing Reena reading it alone.

qa.q: What did Joseph's message change?
qa.a: One calm line reminding everyone that Reena was reading gave Farzana the courage to agree and led the admin to delete the poll, breaking the silence.

qa.q: What was the night like for Reena?
qa.a: Reena was alone in her room reading a pile-on about herself and crying, until a classmate spoke up and the warden called her.

grounding: Shows a student who watches a hostel group pile on a classmate, waits for someone else, and then breaks the silence with one calm message.

passage:
The only signal in Hansa's village came near the water tank behind the panchayat office, so that's where she stood at dusk, phone held high. The college group had 212 members, and tonight it was all about Arohi's speech from English Day: a still of her mid-word, mouth wide, with new captions pasted on it every few minutes: 'Me explaining responsibility to my goat.' 'Arohi when the mic is on.'
Laughing faces, then more. Hansa scrolled. Surely Manpreet, the class rep, would say something. Or one of the toppers. Someone.
Twenty minutes passed. Nobody did. Another caption appeared.
Her mother called from the courtyard that the rotis were getting cold.
Hansa typed, deleted, typed again: 'Arohi practised this for a week. It's not funny to me. Please stop.'
She sent it and went in to eat. When she came back to the tank, Manpreet had written, 'Hansa's right. Enough.' Below it, the first poster had typed, 'Sorry, Arohi. Took it too far.'

qa.q: Where does Hansa go to get signal in her village?
qa.a: She goes near the water tank behind the panchayat office.

qa.q: What was Hansa thinking during the twenty minutes of scrolling?
qa.a: Hansa felt hesitant and kept expecting someone else, Manpreet the class rep or one of the toppers, to speak up; with 212 members it felt as if it could not be her job.

qa.q: Which choice changed the group chat, and why did it work?
qa.a: Hansa's short, calm message naming Arohi's effort and asking the group to stop; once one person spoke, Manpreet backed it up and the first poster apologised to Arohi.

qa.q: What might the evening have been like for Arohi before and after Hansa's message?
qa.a: Before, Arohi would have watched laughing faces pile up with nobody on her side; after, she could see Hansa and Manpreet stand up for her and read an apology from the poster.

grounding: A student watching a large group mock a classmate waits for someone else to speak, then posts one calm message that breaks the silence.

subtopic: Moral disengagement: displacing and diffusing responsibility
passage:
Monday's statistics lecture at the university in Toronto was online because of a snowstorm, ninety-three students in little boxes. Fatima's camera switched on by accident while she was eating soup, and before she noticed, someone had taken a screenshot.
The side chat lit up: 'soup queen', a slurping sound effect, the screenshot again.
Mateo watched from his kitchen table. The TA is in this call, he thought. Somebody will say something. He waited through two slides. The jokes kept coming, and Fatima's box went black.
He unmuted, heart thumping, and kept his voice level. 'Hey, can we drop the screenshot? Anyone's camera could do that. Let's get back to the slides.'
A second of silence. Then the TA: 'Thanks, Mateo. Please delete it.' A few messages appeared: 'yeah, sorry.'
After class, Mateo messaged Fatima: 'That was rough. You okay?'

qa.q: What was Fatima doing when her camera switched on by accident?
qa.a: She was eating soup.

qa.q: Why did Mateo wait through two slides before speaking?
qa.a: Mateo felt hesitant, assuming the TA or somebody among the ninety-three would deal with it; with so many people watching, it felt as if it was not his job.

qa.q: What choice did Mateo make, and how did it change the call?
qa.a: He chose to unmute and calmly ask everyone to drop the screenshot, noting anyone's camera could do that; the TA backed him and others apologised.

qa.q: If you were Fatima, what would Mateo's message after class mean to you?
qa.a: It would show that at least one person saw how awful the moment was and cared; after the jokes, a simple 'You okay?' could make it feel less lonely. 🤍

grounding: A student in a large online class waits for someone else to stop a pile-on, then speaks up calmly himself and others follow.
